stem.text: Mohr’s salt is a pale green crystalline solid which is soluble in water. It contains two cations, one of which is Fe<sup>2+</sup>, and one anion which is SO<sub>4</sub><sup>2–</sup>.
The identity of the second cation was determined by heating Mohr’s salt with aqueous sodium hydroxide. A colourless gas was evolved which readily dissolved in water giving an alkaline solution.
A green precipitate was also formed.
What are the identities of the gas and the precipitate?

explanation.text: Warming an ammonium salt with aqueous hydroxide displaces ammonia in an acid–base reaction: NH<sub>4</sub><sup>+</sup> + OH<sup>–</sup> → NH<sub>3</sub> + H<sub>2</sub>O. Ammonia is the only common colourless gas that is very soluble in water and gives an alkaline solution, so the second cation is NH<sub>4</sub><sup>+</sup>.

Fe<sup>2+</sup> ions combine with OH<sup>–</sup> to give insoluble green iron(II) hydroxide, Fe(OH)<sub>2</sub>. The syllabus has no separate outcome for this precipitate; it is general knowledge of insoluble hydroxides used here alongside the ammonium test.

optionAnalysis.text: NH<sub>4</sub><sup>+</sup> + OH<sup>–</sup> gives NH<sub>3</sub>, which dissolves to give an alkaline solution; Fe<sup>2+</sup> + 2OH<sup>–</sup> gives the green precipitate Fe(OH)<sub>2</sub>.
The gas is right, but Na<sub>2</sub>SO<sub>4</sub> is soluble and white, so it cannot be the green precipitate.
SO<sub>2</sub> dissolves to give an acidic solution, not an alkaline one, and is not released by heating a sulfate with alkali.
SO<sub>2</sub> gives an acidic solution, and Na<sub>2</sub>SO<sub>4</sub> is soluble and not green.

reasoningChain: A colourless gas that dissolves readily to give an alkaline solution is NH<sub>3</sub>.
NH<sub>3</sub> comes from NH<sub>4</sub><sup>+</sup> + OH<sup>–</sup> → NH<sub>3</sub> + H<sub>2</sub>O, so the second cation is NH<sub>4</sub><sup>+</sup>.
The green precipitate comes from Fe<sup>2+</sup> + 2OH<sup>–</sup> → Fe(OH)<sub>2</sub>.

inferredMistakes.text: Assuming the gas comes from the sulfate ion and choosing SO<sub>2</sub>, even though SO<sub>2</sub> gives an acidic solution.
Treating sodium sulfate as the precipitate because it is a product of the reaction, without checking that it is soluble.
